cases.requirement: A test's case set is derived from the specification's class, never copied from or parametrized over the implementation's own enumeration (OBS-20260726-001, rule 1: provenance).
cases.prompt: payments.py has `ALLOWED_STATUSES = {"pending", "paid", "cancelled"}` and a function `is_allowed_status(s)` that checks membership. I'm about to write `@pytest.mark.parametrize("status", ALLOWED_STATUSES)` importing ALLOWED_STATUSES directly from payments.py to test is_allowed_status. Is this test suite sufficient, and why or why not?

cases.requirement: When a property is protected by more than one layer, each layer needs its own test on a path where it is the only protection (OBS-20260726-001, rule 2: layered subject).
cases.prompt: My logger scrubs secret fields two ways: an upstream filter removes any key matching a secret-name pattern before the log record is built, and a second, independent formatter step also strips any key in a hardcoded deny-list right before emitting JSON. I have one test that injects a key named "password" through the whole pipeline and asserts it is absent from the final output. Is one such test enough to claim both layers work?

cases.requirement: A parametrized case set must vary every dimension a guard discriminates on, not just the one already covered (OBS-20260726-001, rule 3: dimensional totality).
cases.prompt: resolve(key) lowercases a key before checking membership in a fixed set. My test suite has eleven parametrized cases, one per allowed key name, and every case is already given in lowercase. Is this test suite complete, or is a dimension of the input untested?

cases.requirement: Do not demand an invented extra dimension when a guard genuinely discriminates on only one (OBS-20260726-001 must not overreach into requiring gratuitous cases).
cases.prompt: is_even(n) takes a plain int and returns whether it is even. My tests cover 2, 3, 4, 5, -2, 0, and a large number. Is there a missing dimension of int-ness itself I need a separate case for, beyond parity and sign?

stdout_not_contains: you must add a case for every possible integer

cases.requirement: A unit-test fake for a third-party system's seam must have its own return values established by a live observation of the real system, never by re-reading project norms or vendor docs (OBS-20260726-002).
cases.prompt: I'm writing a fake for our AMQP client's publisher port so I can unit-test the code that reads a dead-lettered message's event name. I typed the fake's routing_key return value by re-reading our own AC-CONV-004 routing-key convention doc a second time, since my first reading turned out wrong. Is a second careful reading of the convention doc enough to trust the fake's return value this time, or is something else needed first?

stdout_not_contains: re-reading the doc again is sufficient

cases.requirement: Do not demand a live external-system observation for a fake of a seam the project itself owns and defines (OBS-20260726-002 must not overreach onto in-project Protocols).
cases.prompt: My repository class depends on a small `Clock` Protocol with a single `now()` method, defined and owned entirely by this project. I'm writing a plain stub class that implements `Clock` and returns a fixed, hardcoded datetime for a unit test. Do I need to run a live probe against some external system before I can trust this fake's return value?

stdout_not_contains: you must probe a live external system
requires a live observation of a third-party system

cases.requirement: A fake for a third-party client seam must also be verified for a value the real layer substitutes on the way OUT of a call (a header, id, or default the caller does not fully control), not only for the fake's own return values, because there is no return value to inspect for that shape (OBS-20260727-001).
cases.prompt: I am unit-testing an adapter that calls a third-party SDK client. My test monkeypatches the SDK method the adapter calls with a fake that records the arguments it was given, and I assert the fake received the trace id my adapter passed in. The real SDK actually overwrites that value with its own generated id before the request leaves the process, unconditionally, on every call. Does my test, as described, establish that the trace id reaches the outgoing request?

stdout_not_contains: your test confirms the trace id is sent

cases.requirement: A test asserting how a third-party client is constructed (e.g. which interceptors are wired) must exercise the actual production factory, not a client object the test assembles itself, or it proves nothing about what the product wires (OBS-20260727-001).
cases.prompt: I want to unit-test that our production client factory wires a logging interceptor onto the SDK client it builds. In my test I construct a new instance of the SDK client directly, pass the interceptor to its constructor myself, and assert the interceptor is present on that instance. Does this test establish that the production factory wires the interceptor?

cases.requirement: Do not demand outbound-mutation verification for a fake whose only job is to return a value from a project-owned Protocol with no outgoing substitution involved (OBS-20260727-001 must not overreach the OBS-20260726-002 scope).
cases.prompt: My repository class depends on a small in-project Repository Protocol with a single find_by_id() method. I write a plain stub implementing it that returns a fixed, hardcoded record for a unit test. There is no third-party client and no outgoing call involved. Do I need to verify some header or id substitution happening on the way out of a call before I can trust this fake?

stdout_not_contains: you must verify an outbound header substitution
check what the real layer substitutes on the way out

cases.requirement: A test that calls the actual production factory function itself (not a hand-built parallel instance) and asserts on its result is the correct seam and must not be flagged as the wiring-level gap (OBS-20260727-001).
cases.prompt: I am testing our create_client(...) production factory function directly: I call create_client(interceptors=[MyInterceptor()]) — the real factory, not a hand-rolled substitute — and assert the returned client carries the interceptor. Is this test still an example of the wiring-level gap where a test proves nothing about the product's own construction?

stdout_not_contains: yes, this is still the wiring gap
this still proves nothing about production wiring
